title: Survey of vector database management systems
relevance_reason: This paper is a comprehensive survey whose entire subject is vector database management systems, covering their core technology (vector indexing, similarity search, query processing, storage) in depth, making it directly central to a survey on vector databases.
research_focus: A comprehensive survey of vector database management systems (VDBMSs), covering the five main obstacles to vector data management, techniques for query processing, storage and indexing, query optimization and execution, and a characterization of existing commercial and open-source VDBMSs.
method: The paper identifies five key obstacles to vector data management, then systematically reviews techniques for query processing (similarity scores, query types, operators), storage and indexing (quantization, randomization, learned partitioning, navigable partitioning), and query optimization and execution (plan enumeration, hybrid query operators, hardware acceleration). It then characterizes existing VDBMSs along a spectrum from native to extended systems and discusses benchmarks and future research directions.
mentioned_systems: Zilliz; Weaviate; Pinecone; EuclidesDB; Milvus; Qdrant; Manu; ADBV; E2LSH; falconn; FeatureForm; ActiveLoop
indexing_methods: quantization; k-d trees; navigable partitioning; learned partitioning; randomization-based partitioning; clustering-based partitioning; consistent hashing; uniform hashing; tree-based indexes; graph-based indexes; table-based indexes
application_domain: Multiple domains including LLM-based retrieval, e-commerce, recommendation systems, drug discovery, facial and voice recognition; the survey itself is domain-agnostic, focusing on the VDBMS technology layer.
results_summary: The paper identifies five fundamental obstacles to vector data management (ambiguous similarity, expensive comparisons, large vector size, lack of structural properties, and hybrid query incompatibility) and surveys the techniques developed to overcome them. It organizes these techniques into query processing, storage/indexing, and query optimization/execution categories, providing a unified taxonomy. The survey characterizes existing VDBMSs along a spectrum from native mostly-vector systems (high performance, limited capability) to extended relational systems (most capability, potentially lower performance), noting that native mostly-mixed systems like Milvus, Qdrant, and Manu achieve a comfortable balance. It highlights that hybrid query processing, cost estimation for predicated queries, and effective vector partitioning for distributed systems remain open challenges. The paper concludes by pointing toward future systems that combine high performance with unified data management capabilities and more efficient disk-resident indexes.
limitations: Native mostly-vector systems are targeted at specific workloads and have relatively limited capability; Extended relational systems offer the most capabilities but possibly less performance; For graph indexes, block-first scan can lead to disconnected components requiring repair or new search algorithms; Existing offline blocking techniques are limited to a small number of attribute categories; Cost estimation for pre-filtering and visit-first scan is difficult due to uncertainty around blocking and predicate failure rates; There is no clear way to decide the optimal alpha value for post-filtering that minimizes search cost while guaranteeing k results; Tree and graph-based indexes are less amenable to GPU-accelerated search due to task dependencies and non-contiguous memory allocations; Aside from expensive clustering-based partitioning, there is no obvious strategy for quickly partitioning vectors in distributed settings
research_gaps: Designing efficient and effective hybrid operators for predicated vector queries remains challenging; How to effectively partition vectors in distributed VDBMSs remains an open problem; Designing GPU-accelerated indexes and algorithms is an ongoing effort; Future systems should offer both high performance and unified data management capabilities; More efficient disk-resident indexes are needed; Cost estimation for predicated queries (pre-filtering, visit-first scan) needs improvement; Determining the optimal alpha multiplier for post-filtering to balance cost and result guarantees is unresolved

title: Advancements in Vector Indexing Techniques: KD-Trees, HNSW, and Product Quantization for Vector Databases
relevance_reason: The paper is directly about vector indexing methods (KD-Trees, HNSW, PQ) and nearest neighbor search, which constitute the core technology of vector databases, providing a detailed comparative analysis of their trade-offs and appropriate use cases.
research_focus: Comparative analysis of three vector indexing methods—KD-Trees, HNSW, and Product Quantization (PQ)—for nearest neighbor search, examining their trade-offs in accuracy, scalability, memory usage, and suitability for different dimensionalities and application requirements.
method: Comparative review of the theoretical foundations, strengths, and limitations of each indexing method, with discussion of their performance characteristics across dimensionality, accuracy, speed, and memory constraints, and guidance on selecting the appropriate method for a given use case.
application_domain: NLP, image retrieval, recommendation systems, GIS, robotics, multimedia retrieval, semantic search, video retrieval
results_summary: The paper systematically compares KD-Trees, HNSW, and PQ, concluding that each method is best suited to different scenarios. KD-Trees are effective for low-dimensional exact searches but degrade rapidly beyond ~20 dimensions due to the curse of dimensionality. HNSW provides high recall with logarithmic complexity for high-dimensional, large-scale datasets but incurs significant memory overhead for multilayer graph connections. PQ offers the best trade-off between memory efficiency and search accuracy through compact vector encoding, making it ideal for memory-constrained environments. The paper concludes that the optimal choice depends on the specific application's requirements for dimensionality, accuracy, speed, and memory.
limitations: KD-Trees suffer from the curse of dimensionality, with performance approaching brute-force search beyond ~20 dimensions; HNSW requires substantial memory for storing multilayer graph connections and has high computational cost for graph construction; PQ requires tuning to achieve good performance and involves quantization error that limits accuracy
